{{short description|Every triangle with two angle bisectors of equal lengths is isosceles}}
[[File:Steiner lehmus.svg|thumb|right|260px|<math>|AE|=|BD|,\,\alpha=\beta,\,
\gamma=\delta</math> <math>\implies \triangle ABC \text{ is isosceles}</math>]]
The '''Steiner–Lehmus theorem''', a [[theorem]] in [[elementary geometry]], was formulated by [[C. L. Lehmus]] and subsequently [[mathematical proof|proved]] by [[Jakob Steiner]]. It states:

: ''Every [[triangle]] with two [[angle bisector]]s of equal lengths is [[isosceles]]''.

The theorem was first mentioned in 1840 in a letter by C. L. Lehmus to [[Jacques Charles François Sturm|C. Sturm]], in which he asked for a purely geometric proof. Sturm passed the request on to other mathematicians and Steiner was among the first to provide a solution. The theorem became a rather popular topic in elementary geometry ever since with a somewhat regular publication of articles on it.<ref>[[H. S. M. Coxeter|Coxeter, H. S. M.]] and Greitzer, S. L. "The Steiner–Lehmus Theorem." §1.5 in Geometry Revisited. Washington, DC: Math. Assoc. Amer., pp. 14–16, 1967.</ref><ref>Diane and Roy Dowling: [http://www.math.umanitoba.ca/media/ManitobaMathLinks06.pdf ''The Lasting Legacy of Ludolph Lehmus'']. Manitoba Math Links – Volume II – Issue 3, Spring 2002</ref><ref>{{cite journal |jstor=40378432 |title=91.66 Steiner-Lehmus, Revisited |last1=Barbara |first1=Roy |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |year=2007 |volume=91 |issue=522 |pages=528–529 |doi=10.1017/S0025557200182233 |s2cid=125997695 }}</ref>

==Direct proofs==
The Steiner–Lehmus theorem can be proved using elementary geometry by proving the [[contrapositive]] statement: if a triangle is ''not'' isosceles, then it does ''not'' have two angle bisectors of equal length.

There is some controversy over whether a "direct" proof is possible;
allegedly "direct" proofs have been published, but not everyone agrees that these proofs are "direct."
For example, there exist simple [[algebra]]ic expressions for angle bisectors in terms of the sides of the triangle. Equating two of these expressions and algebraically manipulating the equation results in a product of two factors which equal 0, but only one of them (''a''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''b'') can equal 0 and the other must be positive. Thus&nbsp;''a''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''b''. But this may not be considered direct as one must first argue about why the other factor cannot be&nbsp;0.
[[John Horton Conway|John Conway]]<ref>[http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2004-August/008394.html Alleged impossibility of "direct" proof of Steiner–Lehmus theorem]</ref>
has argued that there can be no "equality-chasing" proof because the theorem (stated algebraically) does not hold over an arbitrary [[field (mathematics)|field]], or even when negative [[real number]]s are allowed as parameters.
A precise definition of a "direct proof" inside both [[classical logic|classical]] and [[intuitionistic logic]] has been provided by Victor Pambuccian,<ref name=P>{{citation|first=Victor|last=Pambuccian|title=Negation-free and contradiction-free proof of the Steiner-Lehmus theorem|journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic|volume=59 |year=2018|pages=75–90|doi=10.1215/00294527-2017-0019 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ndjfl/1504252824|url-access=subscription}}.</ref>
who proved, without presenting the direct proofs, that direct proofs must exist in both the classical logic and the intuitionistic logic setting. Ariel Kellison later gave a direct proof.<ref name=Q>{{cite arXiv|first=Ariel|last=Kellison|title=A Machine-Checked Direct Proof of the Steiner-Lehmus Theorem|year=2021|class=cs.LO |eprint=2112.11182 |mode=cs2}}.</ref>
